rationale: A wins because it actually gives the founder four different press lanes, not three versions of regulated-enterprise adoption wearing different jackets. Its “Notion ships offline editing, the feature cloud-native software spent a decade treating as optional” is a real second story; B wrongly buries that by calling “Notion ships offline mode” a standalone “feature note.” B has excellent proof discipline, but “customer/incumbent protagonist” and “consumer-grade tool can pass a bank's security review” both still orbit the same bank-pilot fact.
gaps_in_A: “What it took for a 100M-user productivity app to clear a bank's security review” slightly overstates the evidence. The update says banks run pilots, not that Notion has cleared production security review.

“cloud-native software spent a decade treating as optional” is plausible framing, but it is not in the supplied facts. A handles it better by asking for engineering proof, but the headline still leans on a broad industry claim.
“Data residency comes to the docs app” is useful, but the story type “defensive-comment” is a strange label for an angle that is really regional enterprise-policy news.
gaps_in_B: “Offline editing is real, but on its own it's a feature note” is the bad miss. Offline-first editing with sync at ~100M-user scale is a legitimate product/infrastructure story, not just garnish for compliance.

“collaboration tools have historically lost regulated finance to locked-down incumbents” invents category history and competitive context the update did not provide. That is a reporting hypothesis, not a fact to build the angle on.
“category power shift” is consultant fog. Four bank pilots are interesting; they do not prove a power shift.

The first and third angles duplicate the same core story: bank pilots plus regulated security gate. “Notion says four of the five largest US banks...” and “Notion bets a 100-million-user consumer-grade tool can pass a bank's security review” are different headlines for the same buyer-adoption spine.
